title: 2 Samuel 22:32–51
context: The final stanza celebrates God as the incomparable rock who strengthens David for battle, subdues his enemies, sets him over nations, and shows loving kindness to his anointed and his offspring forever.

verses.text: For who is God, besides the LORD? Who is a rock, besides our God?
verses.arminianNotes: “For who is God, besides the LORD? Who is a rock, besides our God?” Arminian readers see a confession of God’s uniqueness that grounds exclusive trust in him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God confessed as incomparable. The rhetorical questions affirm that no other power can offer the refuge the LORD provides.

verses.text: God is my strong fortress. He makes my way perfect.
verses.arminianNotes: “God is my strong fortress. He makes my way perfect.” Arminian readers see God guiding and strengthening the one who walks with him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God making David’s way secure. Many in this tradition connect this with God’s active work in shaping the life of his servant.

verses.text: He makes his feet like hinds’ feet, and sets me on my high places.
verses.arminianNotes: “He makes his feet like hinds’ feet, and sets me on my high places.” Arminian readers see God granting agility and security in dangerous terrain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God establishing David safely. The image of sure-footed deer conveys stability given by God amid danger.

verses.text: He teaches my hands to war, so that my arms bend a bow of bronze.
verses.arminianNotes: “He teaches my hands to war, so that my arms bend a bow of bronze.” Arminian readers see God equipping his servant for the tasks he is called to.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God training and strengthening David. The verse credits even military skill to God’s instruction and provision.

verses.text: You have also given me the shield of your salvation. Your gentleness has made me great.
verses.arminianNotes: “You have also given me the shield of your salvation. Your gentleness has made me great.” Arminian readers see God’s kindness as the source of David’s greatness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s gentle care exalting his servant. The phrase emphasizes grace rather than human achievement as the key to David’s success.

verses.text: You have enlarged my steps under me. My feet have not slipped.
verses.arminianNotes: “You have enlarged my steps under me. My feet have not slipped.” Arminian readers see God providing room and stability for faithful living.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s preserving care. The image of secure footing expresses confidence in God’s protection along the path he sets.

verses.text: I have pursued my enemies and destroyed them. I didn’t turn again until they were consumed.
verses.arminianNotes: “I have pursued my enemies and destroyed them.” Arminian readers see the language of ancient warfare used to describe victories God granted David over real enemies.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the verse within David’s historical battles. Readers in this tradition generally apply such language today to God’s triumph over evil rather than to personal enemies.

verses.text: I have consumed them, and struck them through, so that they can’t arise. Yes, they have fallen under my feet.
verses.arminianNotes: “I have consumed them, and struck them through, so that they can’t arise.” Arminian readers see the completeness of the victory God gave his servant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see decisive deliverance described in vivid warrior language. The verse celebrates God’s faithfulness in giving victory over persistent threats.

verses.text: For you have armed me with strength for the battle. You have subdued under me those who rose up against me.
verses.arminianNotes: “For you have armed me with strength for the battle.” Arminian readers see God strengthening his servant, who still had to fight faithfully.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God as the source of victory. The verse returns credit to God, making clear that David’s triumphs depended on divine empowerment.

verses.text: You have also made my enemies turn their backs to me, that I might cut off those who hate me.
verses.arminianNotes: “You have also made my enemies turn their backs to me.” Arminian readers see God giving David success over those who opposed him and God’s purposes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God subduing enemies before his king. The verse continues the pattern of attributing victory to God rather than human skill.

verses.text: They looked, but there was no one to save; even to the LORD, but he didn’t answer them.
verses.arminianNotes: “They looked, but there was no one to save; even to the LORD, but he didn’t answer them.” Arminian readers see enemies calling on God too late, after setting themselves against him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God refusing to save those who opposed his anointed. The verse contrasts with verse 7, where God heard David’s cry.

verses.text: Then I beat them as small as the dust of the earth. I crushed them as the mire of the streets, and spread them abroad.
verses.arminianNotes: “Then I beat them as small as the dust of the earth.” Arminian readers see poetic hyperbole celebrating complete victory granted by God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see vivid language for decisive triumph. The imagery belongs to ancient victory songs and expresses God’s thorough deliverance.

verses.text: You also have delivered me from the strivings of my people. You have kept me to be the head of the nations. A people whom I have not known will serve me.
verses.arminianNotes: “You have kept me to be the head of the nations.” Arminian readers see God establishing David’s rule beyond Israel and delivering him from internal strife.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God exalting his king over nations. Many readers in this tradition see this as anticipating a wider reign fulfilled ultimately in the Messiah.

verses.text: The foreigners will submit themselves to me. As soon as they hear of me, they will obey me.
verses.arminianNotes: “The foreigners will submit themselves to me. As soon as they hear of me, they will obey me.” Arminian readers see God’s blessing extending David’s influence to other peoples.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the nations coming under God’s king. The verse expresses confidence that God’s purposes for David’s reign reach beyond Israel’s borders.

verses.text: The foreigners will fade away, and will come trembling out of their close places.
verses.arminianNotes: “The foreigners will fade away, and will come trembling out of their close places.” Arminian readers see the collapse of resistance before the king God has established.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s power humbling enemies. The imagery of trembling surrender concludes the description of victory before the final praise.

verses.text: The LORD lives! Blessed be my rock! Exalted be God, the rock of my salvation,
verses.arminianNotes: “The LORD lives! Blessed be my rock! Exalted be God, the rock of my salvation.” Arminian readers see joyful praise to the living God who delivers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the song returning to its opening image of God as rock. The verse is shared ground: the living God is praised as the source of salvation.

verses.text: even the God who executes vengeance for me, who brings down peoples under me,
verses.arminianNotes: The song praises “the God who executes vengeance for me, who brings down peoples under me.” Arminian readers see God acting justly on behalf of his servant rather than David seeking personal revenge.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see vengeance belonging to God. The verse reflects David’s restraint toward Saul, leaving judgment in God’s hands.

verses.text: who brings me away from my enemies. Yes, you lift me up above those who rise up against me. You deliver me from the violent man.
verses.arminianNotes: “You deliver me from the violent man.” Arminian readers see God rescuing his servant from those who sought his harm, including Saul.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God lifting David above his enemies. The verse summarizes the deliverances celebrated throughout the song.

verses.text: Therefore I will give thanks to you, LORD, among the nations, and will sing praises to your name.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore I will give thanks to you, LORD, among the nations, and will sing praises to your name.” Arminian readers see praise reaching beyond Israel to the nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s name proclaimed among the nations. Romans 15:9 cites the parallel verse in Psalm 18 in connection with the Gentiles glorifying God.

verses.text: He gives great deliverance to his king, and shows loving kindness to his anointed, to David and to his offspring, forever more.”
verses.arminianNotes: “He gives great deliverance to his king, and shows loving kindness to his anointed, to David and to his offspring, forever more.” Arminian readers see God’s faithful love promised to David’s line.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the covenant of 2 Samuel 7 echoed here. Many readers in both traditions see this promise fulfilled ultimately in Christ, the Son of David.
